result:
Both integrate changes from one branch into another; they differ in how they treat history.

**`git merge`** ties the two branches together with a new merge commit that has both as parents. Existing commits are untouched.

```
A---B---C  main
     \       \
      D---E---M  feature (after merging main in)
```

**`git rebase`** replays your commits one by one on top of the other branch, creating new commits with new hashes. The result is a straight line, as if you had started your work from the latest tip.

```
A---B---C  main
         \
          D'---E'  feature (after rebasing onto main)
```

| | Merge | Rebase |
|---|---|---|
| History | Preserved exactly, with branch points visible | Rewritten to be linear |
| Commit hashes | Unchanged | Changed for the replayed commits |
| Conflicts | Resolved once, in the merge commit | Possibly resolved repeatedly, once per replayed commit |
| Safe on shared branches | Yes | No |

**Rule of thumb:**
- Rebase your own local, unpushed work to tidy it up or bring it up to date with `main` before opening a PR.
- Merge when integrating into a shared branch, or when others have already pulled the commits involved.

Never rebase commits other people have based work on. Their history will then diverge from yours, and sorting it out is painful. If you rebase a branch you've already pushed, you'll need `git push --force-with-lease`, which is fine on a branch only you use.

A related option is `git merge --squash`, which collapses a whole branch into a single commit on the target. That gives linear history without rewriting the source branch's commits.
